cues.text: Hello and welcome to today’s talk. Here with me is the famous botanist.
cues.speaker: Host

cues.text: Professor Alison Downing. So, Alison, tell us something about cocoa beans.
cues.speaker: Host

cues.text: Cocoa beans, also called cacao beans, are the primary constituent in making chocolate.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Grown in tropical areas in South and Central America, West Africa and Asia, the cocoa tree is often raised on small, family-owned farms.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: When the harvested pods are opened to expose the beans, the pulp and cocoa seeds are removed and the rind is discarded.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The pulp and seeds are then piled in heaps, placed in bins, or laid out on grates for several days.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: During this time, the seeds and pulp undergo a process called ‘sweating’, where the thick pulp liquefies as it ferments.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The fermented pulp trickles away, leaving cocoa seeds behind to be collected.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: This is when the beans are harvested and then the bags holding them are ready to be transported.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: But the most important step in processing the cocoa bean is cleaning it.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Once the beans are unloaded from the railroad cars, the packages are opened and then weighed by machines.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Then the pods are split, and the seeds or beans are covered with a sweet white pulp or mucilage.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: On arrival at the factory, the cocoa beans are sorted and put in a hopper to be cleaned more rigorously.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The wet beans are then transported to a facility so they can be fermented and dried.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: They are fermented for 4 to 7 days and must be mixed every 2 days.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: They are dried for 5 to 14 days, depending on the climate conditions.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The fermented beans are dried by spreading them out over a large surface and constantly raking them.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Then the beans are ready to be roasted. Now, roasting takes place at a high temperature and then the beans are boiled in a heated chamber.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: During the roasting process the beans will be expanded and cracked.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: But prior to this, the beans are trodden and shuffled about using bare human feet
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: During this process, red clay mixed with water is sprinkled over the beans to obtain a finer colour, polish, and protection against molds during shipment to factories in the United States, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and other countries.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Now, back to what I was saying. After the beans are cracked, they need to be cooled.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Then the roasted beans are sealed in pockets.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Wow, that is not a simple process, is it? But someone told me that different roasting levels of coffee can lead to different kind of flavours.
cues.speaker: Host

cues.text: Yes. Roasting coffee transforms the chemical and physical properties of green coffee beans into roasted coffee products.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The roasting process is what produces the characteristic flavour of coffee by causing the green coffee beans to change in taste.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Unroasted beans contain similar if not higher levels of acids, protein, sugars, and caffeine as those that have been roasted, but lack the taste of roasted coffee beans due to the Maillard and other chemical reactions that occur during roasting.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: The vast majority of coffee is roasted commercially on a large scale, but small-scale commercial roasting has grown significantly with the trend toward ‘single-origin’ coffees served at specialty shops.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Some coffee drinkers even roast coffee at home as a hobby in order to both experiment with the flavour profile of the beans and ensure the freshest possible roast.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: So here, I am going to introduce some of these roasted coffee beans and their special flavours.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Now, the First Crack is lighter-bodied, and has a higher acidity level with no obvious roast flavour, and is popular for its special mild taste.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: This level of roast is ideal for tasting the full original character of the coffee. The Green Beans are raw, unroasted coffee beans.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: They are strictly hard beans with a smoky flavour and are slightly acidic.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: We’ve also got French Roast. And the flavour that comes across in French roast coffee usually has more to do with the roasting process than the actual quality of the beans.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: By the time the beans are dark enough to qualify as French, most of their original flavour has dissipated.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: In its place come the flavours of caramelising sugar, bittersweet coffee, and often,  a bit of chocolate.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: And finally, Espresso Smoky. That is coffee brewed by forcing a small amount of nearly boiling water under pressure through finely ground coffee beans.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Espresso is generally thicker than coffee brewed through other methods, has a higher concentration of suspended and dissolved solids, and has crema on top.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: As a result of the pressurised brewing process, the flavours and chemicals in a typical cup of espresso are very concentrated.
cues.speaker: Alison

cues.text: Espresso is also the base for other drinks such as a cafe latte, cappuccino, cafe macchiato, cafe mocha, flat white,
cues.speaker: Alison
